title: “His diaper has been dry since morning”
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; the unit’s pediatric protocol, formulary and the attending pediatric nephrologist decide every order. No doses are given.
intro:
You are the attending pediatric nephrologist. At 9 p.m. a pediatric resident at a district hospital in San Jose, Nueva Ecija, calls about Gabriel Manalastas, 2 years old, 12 kg. Six days ago he had watery diarrhea that turned bloody, and the family gave a loperamide syrup from the pharmacy. Today he is pale, puffy and drowsy, and his diaper has been dry for 18 hours. The smear shows fragmented red cells.

The admitting orders already list intravenous ciprofloxacin, a platelet transfusion and furosemide “for oliguria.” His mother, Rowena, is beside the bed.

n1.prompt: What do you tell the resident about the orders?

choices.text: This is Shiga toxin HUS until proven otherwise. Stop the ciprofloxacin and the loperamide, hold the platelets, avoid nephrotoxins, and treat the potassium now by the unit’s protocol.
choices.feedback: Bloody diarrhea, then hemolysis with fragmented cells, low platelets and anuric AKI (acute kidney injury) is STEC-HUS (Shiga toxin–producing E. coli hemolytic uremic syndrome) until shown otherwise. Antibiotics for the diarrhea alone and antimotility drugs are avoided; platelets are held unless he bleeds or needs a procedure. The potassium cannot wait for the transfer.

choices.text: Stop the ciprofloxacin, but give the platelets anyway, since 34,000 is low before a catheter.
choices.feedback: Stopping the antibiotic is right. Platelets are held in HUS unless there is bleeding or a procedure is actually under way; giving them now adds risk without a clear benefit. The procedure team can decide when the time comes.
choices.then: You hold the platelets after all and ask the resident to treat the potassium by protocol.

choices.text: Keep the orders and add a second dose of furosemide to get the urine going.
choices.feedback: An anuric kidney in HUS will not answer to furosemide, and waiting for it delays the real decision. The ciprofloxacin and loperamide stay in a child whose illness they may worsen, and the potassium goes untreated.
choices.then: An hour later there is still no urine and the potassium is 6.4 mmol/L. You call back, stop the harmful orders and ask for potassium treatment by protocol.

n2.scene: The district hospital cannot dialyze a 12 kg child. The nearest pediatric unit that can is in Manila, about three hours by ambulance.
n2.prompt: Where should Gabriel be treated tonight?

choices.text: Transfer tonight. Call the accepting pediatric nephrologist and intensivist yourself, agree what is done before the ambulance leaves, and send a written endorsement.
choices.feedback: An anuric, hyperkalemic, hypertensive and drowsy child with HUS needs a bed where dialysis can start the same day and his brain can be watched. A doctor-to-doctor call and a short written plan (potassium treated, harmful orders stopped, blood pressure, a working intravenous line) make a three-hour ride safer.

choices.text: Send him to Manila by ambulance tonight, and let the resident make the calls.
choices.feedback: The destination is right, but the handoff is the weak link. An accepting team that hears about a drowsy anuric toddler from the ambulance crew may have no bed and no PD catheter ready.
choices.then: The receiving resident calls you at 23:30, unsure whether a dialysis bed is free. You call the attending there and confirm acceptance.

choices.text: Keep him overnight, repeat the labs in the morning, and decide then.
choices.feedback: He already meets indications for urgent dialysis (no urine, rising potassium, drowsiness). Waiting until morning in a hospital that cannot dialyze him spends the hours he does not have.
choices.then: At 02:00 he is harder to rouse. You arrange urgent transfer by phone, three hours later than it could have been.

n3.scene: Gabriel is in the pediatric intensive care unit. He has gained 600 g, has made no urine, and needs blood. The surgical team can place a PD catheter this morning; a hemodialysis catheter and a pediatric circuit are also possible.

choices.text: Acute peritoneal dialysis, with a transfusion given on dialysis to make room for it.
choices.feedback: Acute PD needs no vascular access and no blood prime, removes fluid gently, and avoids systemic anticoagulation in a toddler with very low platelets. Dialysis also makes room for blood and nutrition.

HD works and is the choice when PD is not possible, for example after abdominal surgery or with a PD leak. In a 12 kg child with low platelets it means a central catheter, a primed circuit and anticoagulation decisions that PD avoids.
choices.then: The team agrees PD is simpler for him, and the catheter goes in that morning.

choices.text: Wait another day for urine, with furosemide every six hours.
choices.feedback: Indications are already met. In HUS the kidney recovers over days to weeks; furosemide does not bring that forward, and waiting lets potassium, fluid and uremia build.
choices.then: By noon his potassium is 6.8 mmol/L. PD starts that afternoon.

n4.scene: He is stable on PD. But the hemolysis has not settled: platelets are still about 30,000/µL and LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) is still high a week in. The stool Shiga toxin test came back negative, and his C3 is low. Rowena mentions that a cousin had “kidney trouble with low blood” as a baby.

choices.text: Think atypical HUS. Store serum and EDTA plasma for complement studies, anti-factor H antibodies, genetics and ADAMTS13 before any plasma, then start the access process for C5 blockade, with plasma as a bridge.
choices.feedback: Persistent hemolysis after the first week, a low C3, a negative stool test and a family history point to complement-mediated (atypical) HUS. Samples drawn after plasma are hard to interpret, so draw them first. C5 blockade is the disease-specific treatment; in the Philippines access takes time, so start the request now.

choices.text: Start plasma exchange today and send the complement studies afterward.
choices.feedback: Plasma therapy is a reasonable bridge, but samples drawn afterward may miss or mask the defect. Store the samples first; it takes minutes.
choices.then: The intensivist delays the first exchange by an hour so the samples can be drawn.

choices.text: Continue supportive care. STEC-HUS sometimes takes longer to settle.
choices.feedback: Some STEC-HUS is slow, but here several clues point the other way. Missing atypical HUS delays the one treatment that can save his kidneys and prevent relapse.
choices.then: On day 11 the platelets fall further. The team sends complement studies and starts the request for C5 blockade.

end.title: Week 6
end.text: Gabriel is off dialysis, with a creatinine still above normal for his age. Genetic results are pending, and the family has been counseled about relapse, vaccination and long-term follow-up of blood pressure, urine protein and kidney function. The endorsement letter to his home hospital lists what to watch for and who to call.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Bloody diarrhea, then hemolysis, low platelets and AKI is STEC-HUS until proven otherwise. Stop antibiotics given for the diarrhea alone, antimotility drugs and routine platelets.
  • Treat what kills first: potassium, overload, hypertension and seizures.
  • Choose the bed, not just the drug. An anuric, drowsy child needs same-day dialysis and brain monitoring, arranged doctor to doctor.
  • Acute PD suits a toddler with low platelets.
  • Think atypical when hemolysis persists past the first week, C3 is low, or the family history fits; store samples before plasma.

See the module sections above and Module 16 for acute dialysis in the PICU.
